steps.title: Open the authorities
steps.body: The Certification Authorities entry of the PKI menu opens the CA inventory, with three views: table, hierarchy and graph.
steps.note: The data was prepared through the API before recording, with synthetic names and a unique suffix per run.

steps.title: Initial state
steps.body: The table shows four CAs, three of them top-level: Demo-Hybrid-A, Demo-Hybrid-B and an unrelated root. The issuing CA sits under B. No certificate links A to B yet.
steps.note: The unrelated root has no relationship with A or B and serves as the wrong anchor in the external tests.

steps.title: Open Cross Sign
steps.body: The form issues an existing CA a second certificate signed by another CA. The target CA keeps its key and its subject.
steps.note: Both CAs need their private key in the KMS: the picker only offers active CAs whose key is available.

steps.title: Choose the signer
steps.body: The picker lists the CAs with their hierarchy. The CA chosen here becomes the issuer of the new certificate.
steps.note: The CA names of this run carry a unique suffix so that every repetition is independent.

steps.title: A as signer
steps.body: A will sign with its private key. In the A → B notation, A issues a CA certificate for B.
steps.note: A does not change: it remains a self-signed root.

steps.title: Choose the target
steps.body: The target is the CA whose key pair receives a second certificate. The list excludes the CA already chosen as signer.

steps.title: B as target
steps.body: B is the root that has the issuing CA beneath it. The cross certificate reuses B's key, so what B already issued chains through either issuer.
steps.note: After signing there will be two entries named B; later tests tell them apart by issuer and serial number.

steps.title: Cross certificate preview
steps.body: The form shows Subject, Issuer, Public key, Subject Key ID and Authority Key ID of the resulting certificate. The public key is listed as reused from B.
steps.note: This is the form's preview, not a validation: key identity is checked afterwards on the PEM files.

steps.title: Cross certificate expiry
steps.body: By default the cross certificate expires like the target CA, capped by the signer. A duration is chosen so that the validity of the A → B link is visible.
steps.note: A path's validity is bounded by the certificate that expires first.

steps.title: 3-year duration
steps.body: The field takes a number followed by a unit (y, w, d, h, m, s). With 3y the cross certificate expires before root B and before its issuing CA.
steps.note: The A → B link stops being usable before B itself; the direct path from B does not depend on it.

steps.title: Issue A → B
steps.body: Lamassu stores the result as a new CA entry and opens its page. The original, self-signed B is not replaced.
steps.note: The operation is real: it changes the server. That is why every run starts from an empty instance.

steps.title: Cross certificate page
steps.body: The page of the new entry names the CA B and shows A as issuer, with a validity period of about three years from issuance.
steps.note: Only the issuance is observed here. Whether the path validates is an external check, not a UI action.

steps.title: Back to the inventory
steps.body: The inventory now includes the new entry. It is reviewed in the three views: table, hierarchy and graph.

steps.title: Table after the cross-signing
steps.body: The table now has five CAs. B is listed as a self-signed root and as a subordinate of A; the 'Expires vs. parent' column compares each subordinate's expiry with its issuer's.
steps.note: The two B rows are different certificates of the same key.

steps.title: Open the hierarchy
steps.body: The hierarchy draws each CA as a card and joins each issuer with the CAs it issued.

steps.title: B in two positions
steps.body: Arrows go from an issuer to the CAs it issued. B appears under A (cross certificate) and as a root with its issuing CA, so there are two possible paths to the issuing CA.
steps.note: Which path a validator uses depends on the anchors and intermediates it is given. The hierarchy does not draw end-entity identities.

steps.title: Open the graph
steps.body: In the graph each card is a key and its rows are the certificates attesting it; arrows go from the signing key to the certificate it signed.

steps.title: Whole graph
steps.body: B's key gathers two certificates, the self-signed and the cross one, and carries the Cross-signed badge. There is an arrow from A to B and from B to the issuing CA; the unrelated root has none.
steps.note: Long names are truncated on the cards; the table shows the full names. The missing link to the unrelated root explains the validation failure with it as anchor.

steps.title: Filter the cross-signing
steps.body: The Cross-signed filter keeps only the keys whose certificates with the same subject were signed by more than one key, plus the keys that signed them.
steps.note: It is a view filter: it does not change any data.

steps.title: Isolated A → B link
steps.body: A's key signs one of the two certificates of B's key. It is the link that the cross-signing adds.
steps.note: B's other certificate is still the self-signed one.

steps.title: Open Certificates
steps.body: The Certificates list gathers all issued certificates, CA ones included, with their issuer and expiry.

steps.title: Certificates involved
steps.body: Each row shows the certificate with its issuer and expiry. B's two certificates share a name and differ in the CA Issuer column: B and A; the cross one expires earlier.
steps.note: The full serial number appears on each certificate's page.

steps.title: Open the identity
steps.body: The identity is the end-entity certificate whose validity is checked from A.

steps.title: Identity and external validation
steps.body: The page shows B's issuing CA as issuer. The validation from A, done outside the recording, accepted the path identity → issuing → B cross → A when both intermediates were supplied.
steps.note: Without the cross certificate, without the issuing CA, or with the unrelated root as anchor, validation failed; with B as anchor there is a shorter alternative path.
